edgar_fts CLAIM EVOLUTION on DOD OIG audit (Mode B) — CRITICAL FINDING. FY2023 10-K Note 13 explicitly discloses: 'In 2019, the DOD OIG received a congressional letter requesting a comprehensive review of TransDigm's contracts with the DOD from January 2017 through June 2019 to identify whether TransDigm earned excess profits. ... In December 2021, the OIG completed the audit and issued the related audit report. ... the report recommended that TransDigm voluntarily refund at least $21 million in excess profit on 150 contracts ... No loss contingency related to the voluntary refund request has been recorded as of September 30, 2023.' This entire disclosure was DROPPED from the FY2024 10-K and remains absent from the FY2025 10-K Note 13 Commitments and Contingencies. The matter has been quietly omitted without explicit resolution narrative — either the refund was made (no cash-flow disclosure found), the matter was closed (no acknowledgment in subsequent filings), or it has been deemed immaterial. This is a material claim-evolution gap. The 2018 House report (Khanna / Lieu / Cotton bipartisan letter) preceded the OIG audit and is part of TDG's well-documented government pricing controversy history.

Zero mention of 'Inspector General', 'OIG', 'voluntary refund', or '$21 million' in the FY2025 10-K full-text. The matter has been silently omitted.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Material disclosure gap. The DOD OIG audit was a high-profile 2019-2021 congressional inquiry (Khanna/Lieu/Cotton bipartisan letter; the OIG report was the formal Pentagon response). For TDG to disclose it in the FY2023 10-K as an open contingent matter and then silently drop it in FY2024 and FY2025 without explicit resolution disclosure is unusual. Three possibilities: (a) the $21M voluntary refund was negotiated or settled at a sub-material level and TDG management chose not to disclose, (b) the matter was deemed not probable of any loss and accounting materiality dropped it below the disclosure threshold, (c) the matter remains technically open but TDG is no longer disclosing because no new development has occurred. None of these three is necessarily a violation of disclosure rules — TDG's standing 10-K policy is to report governmental matters that exceed $1M monetary sanctions. But for an investor reading the FY2025 10-K cold, the absence of any narrative continuation of a previously-disclosed open contingent matter is a Mode-B catch. The LONG thesis needs to price in (a) potential reactivation of congressional pricing scrutiny if a future GAO/IG audit recurs, (b) TDG's well-documented pattern of pricing models that may face periodic political pressure especially with a new Administration's defense-cost-reduction priorities. NOT escalated to SEVERE because the $21M sum is immaterial against $8.8B revenue and TDG plausibly closed the matter; but the disclosure-evolution gap is real.
